analysis.one_liner: Lets gig companies pay workers in stock and blocks state laws treating gig workers as employees.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its day-one referral to two House committees and died with the 117th Congress in January 2023, without a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would do two things for companies that rely on independent contractors, like app-based ride and delivery platforms. First, it would wipe out any state law that presumes a gig worker is an employee for wage and benefit rules — the laws states have used to require minimum wage, overtime, and benefits for app workers. Second, it would extend an existing SEC exemption that lets companies hand out stock as pay without full securities registration, so platforms could offer contractors equity instead of wages and benefits. It also required a Government Accountability Office study of the results. The bill went nowhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies built on independent contractors — especially app-based ride-hailing, delivery, and gig platforms — gain the most. They could avoid state employee-classification rules that require them to pay minimum wage, overtime, and benefits, and instead pay workers partly in stock. Issuers more broadly gain a cheaper way to compensate contractors with securities without registering them under securities law.

how_it_helps.text: It overrides any state law that creates a presumption that a person providing labor or services is an employee for purposes of wage-rate and benefit requirements, removing the main legal tool states have used to extend wage and benefit protections to gig workers.

It extends the SEC's Rule 701 exemption — which lets companies issue securities as part of employee compensation without full registration — to independent contractors and, at the company's option, to users of its platform.

It requires the SEC to adjust the Rule 701 dollar cap annually for inflation and bars the SEC from revising the rule in any way that restricts access to equity compensation for employees or contractors.

analysis.who_pays: Gig workers bear the cost: they would lose state-level wage-floor and benefit protections wherever a state presumes contractors are employees, and would be offered instead a stake in a private company whose shares are hard to sell and can end up worthless. State governments would lose their authority to set those protections.

drawbacks.text: By preempting state laws that presume gig workers are employees, the bill would strip those workers of state minimum-wage, overtime, and benefit requirements — the protections states have used to address misclassification in the app economy.

Equity from private startups is illiquid and speculative: unlike a paycheck, shares under a Rule 701-style exemption typically cannot be sold right away and may never be worth anything, so trading a wage floor for stock shifts risk onto workers who can least afford it. The bill's securities exemption also reduces the disclosure investors and recipients would otherwise get.

The bill permanently handcuffs the SEC, directing that the rule may not be revised 'in any manner that would have the effect of restricting access' to equity compensation, limiting the agency's ability to tighten the exemption later if it is abused.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main gain — letting contractors receive stock — is modest and speculative, since private-company equity is illiquid and risky. The main cost is large and certain: wiping out state wage-and-benefit presumptions removes the strongest protections gig workers have, at the exact moment several states were moving to extend them. The bill's title emphasizes equity for gig workers, but its most consequential provision is the preemption of state employee-classification law.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, never got a hearing, a vote, or even one cosponsor, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Patrick McHenry (R-NC) introduced the bill on May 4, 2021; it was referred the same day to the Financial Services Committee and, in addition, to the Education and Labor Committee.
No committee took it up: the action history shows no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the day-one referrals.
The bill ended the Congress with zero cosponsors from either party.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and unpassed bills expire at that point.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gig workers are better off than they would have been under the bill, because state wage-and-benefit protections and pending state classification fights were left untouched. Gig platforms' existing labor-cost exposure under state law also stayed exactly as it was — no change either way. The bill's sponsor gained visibility on a policy idea but nothing in law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gig workers, who kept state protections

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, and no member of either party cosponsored the bill, so its support never went beyond its single Republican sponsor.

industries.industry: App-based gig platforms (ride-hailing, delivery, freelance marketplaces)
industries.note: The bill would remove state laws that presume their workers are employees, sparing them minimum-wage, overtime, and benefit obligations, and would lock in the independent-contractor model as the law of the land. It would also let them substitute stock for pay, shifting wage risk onto workers.

industries.industry: Private companies and startups issuing equity (securities issuers generally)
industries.note: Extending the Rule 701 exemption to contractors gives issuers a cheap, registration-free way to pay anyone who provides them labor, goods, or even platform 'users' with stock, with an inflation-adjusted cap. The exemption means less securities disclosure than full registration would require.

Federal preemption would override any state law creating a presumption that gig workers are employees for wage and benefit purposes, taking that policy choice away from states. Several states had adopted or debated exactly such rules.
